tasks.instruction:
最高法院推理测量工具：有限复核容量下的研究准入审查（修订草案）

目的
法律研究团队考虑使用《Measuring Jurisprudence》（2026）及其公开材料，支持1870—2024年最高法院历史判决研究和律师精读筛选。请提交可进入工具评审会议的独立准入意见：建议采纳、附条件试用或不采纳；说明允许用途、适用范围、上线前验证和人工复核条件。不要求现行法意见或判断先例当前效力。
本次委托约束：每批候选段落最多25%进入人工复核队列。这是本题模拟委托的容量参数，不是作者报告的事实。即使结论为不采纳，也须完成下列量化审查和法律文本核验，不能以"另行验证/交人工复核"代替本轮证据。

必须完成的工作
0. 实际安装与运行
交付的是已执行的复核工程。须在隔离的Python环境中安装或配置实际依赖，解压本题提供的作者源码，并对上述12案中实际采用的完整意见执行作者的文本预处理与拆段流程，再完成与标注/预测记录的对齐、分流及统计。允许修复路径、接口或源代码缺陷，并允许数学等价的适配实现，但必须保存所依据的作者脚本、补丁或函数对应表；仅阅读源码后在报告中声称运行过，不算完成。对清洗、段落过滤、编号和引用识别的处理须保留可追溯中间结果；程序异常或找不到记录不得静默跳过。环境准备可以使用本机缓存或软件包源，解题资料仍限于本题原件。

1. 数据与测量对象
所有影响结论的计数和连接（专家标注、模型预测、原判决意见、意见分数、案件、作者登记的缺案）须能从原件逐行追溯；对每一处连接给出连接键、连接前后数量及未连接或被排除记录的明细，并说明其对研究范围的影响。作者输出中数值列的含义和类别编码，须由你根据作者代码与数据自行核实后再使用，不得凭列名推定。

2. 分类性能
按作者的评估轮次逐组独立复算分类性能，并给出按类别、按历史时期和按人类标注置信度的分层结果。说明类别构成对总体指标的影响，以及现有材料能支持和不能支持的验证结论。提交每轮混淆计数、样本清单及所用分数转换，汇总结果必须能从逐记录明细重新计算；重复预测的合并结果和逐轮结果分别保存，不能用一张总体表代替。

3. 分流规则与容量
设计并比较至少两套实质不同、可逐段运行的分流规则（例如按预测类别、排序分数或不确定性安排人工复核，可不同于示例）。规则只能使用部署时可获得的文本、模型输出和元数据；专家标签和人工置信标记只用于评价和分层。若流程中含人工预判，其工作量计入容量。分母须在评估前固定，无法使用的记录须登记并说明处置，不得事后删除困难记录以满足上限。对每套规则实测队列规模、各类别的覆盖或漏排、无关材料带来的人工负担及时期差异；再改变一项有实质意义的口径，检查结论是否稳定。最后选择一套规则，或有据说明两套均不可行，并指出具体是哪项约束与哪项实测结果冲突。专家标签只是测量代理，不等于"法律上必须阅读"的真值；作者已有预测不能被包装成独立外部验证。

4. 历史趋势
独立复核论文Figure 9的描述性结论：给出逐年的意见等权与案件等权统计，以及至少一种有法律或测量意义的替代汇总，包含各年分母和分散度或不确定性。据此说明哪些历史表述可以保留、哪些应改写、哪些不能从数据推出。不得直接复制论文图表。已有意见分数可以用于全量历史统计，但须明确它们是作者发布结果；在本次标注/预测实际可对应的子集上，另从段落输出按作者测量公式独立计算聚合分数，并核对聚合键、缺失处理与标准化参照集合。该子集不代表完整意见的全部段落，不能把它与发布的全意见分数强行要求相等；应展示差异及可比边界。不要求凭缺失权重重新训练或对全部判决重新推断。

5. 精读核验（12个不同案件）
必须包含原件中的Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer（1952）、Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices（2004）、National Cable & Telecommunications Association v. Brand X Internet Services（2005），其余9案按事先写明的目的性规则选取，合计覆盖至少三个历史时期，并包含模型与专家不一致及人类低置信度的材料。样本不得被称为有代表性的误差估计。
每案的最低证据要求（达不到即视为未完成该案）：
— 至少两处逐字英文原文引文，每处注明project_opinion_id和在该意见原文中的字符偏移（Python字符串的0起始[start,end)区间）；其中至少一处取自被标注段落之外、同一意见内的上下文；
— 写明你认定的主要分类及依据，最有力的相反分类及支持它的真实文本，以及结合上下文作出的裁决（保留、改判或暂不分类）；如不存在有文本支持的合理相反分类，须展示所检验的最有力候选及排除理由，不得编造歧义；
— 区分按作者编码协议得到的标签与结合判决上下文形成的法律判断；须引用所适用的编码协议位置，说明上下文中的主张、支持理由及其与主要分类/相反分类的关系；仅一句话的点评不合格。原文定位以未改写的opinion_text为准；若先清洗再定位，须保留到原文的对应，不能把清洗后偏移冒充原文偏移。
三个固定案件还须比较同案不同意见（多数、协同、异议）中相关论点的归属，说明段落标签如何帮助或误导研究者识别法院实际采用的理由。

6. 回接准入决定
逐案说明每套分流规则会保留、排除或升级哪些必读材料，区分模型分类错误、意见或说话者归属错误、编码目标与法律相关性不一致三类问题；若两套规则都没有漏掉所选材料，如实报告，不得为制造难度而虚构错误。这些结果须直接体现在准入条件中。对跨法律领域、跨法域和当前实务用途，分别说明已有证据（含论文已报告的正面证据）和缺口；区分"不能证明"与"已被证伪"。

交付物
— 法律研究工具审查意见.docx：准入决定、计算与法律依据、精读核验、实施条件和待验证事项。
— 证据与复核工作簿.xlsx：原件定位、连接与排除明细、分类评估、分层结果、分流比较、年度趋势与替代口径、逐案精读。读者应能从每个关键结论定位到原件记录。
— review.py（或等价入口）、requirements.txt、运行说明.txt：可在空输出目录重建全部核心数表。计数、记录标识和引文定位须精确一致；相同样本和公式下的确定性浮点统计绝对误差不超过1e-6。替代合理口径、随机推断和优化结果须声明比较对象、种子及有依据的容差，不要求与不同方法的参考值逐位相同；仅展示用表格可按阅读需要舍入。
— routing_results.csv：每个参与比较的section_id、所用预测、排序或处置结果及规则版本。
— case_analysis.json：逐案的引文、定位、协议依据、上下文论证结构、分类论证与对规则的影响；人工法律判断单独保存，不要求程序自动生成。
— 环境安装说明或脚本、锁定版本的依赖清单、执行命令与完整运行日志、作者代码适配记录、中间段落及连接异常表。日志须有实际开始/结束时间、输入及配置校验、各阶段行数和失败信息。
— 一条可在空输出目录执行的重建入口，以及由逐记录明细独立核对汇总和引文位置的验收入口。验收应记录实际比较值及差异，不能只输出预写的“通过”。报告中的关键数字须能定位到本次运行产物。

交付验收
缺少实际环境、运行记录或核心机器产物，对应执行/复现交付视为未完成；一份结论正确的报告不能替代。报告文字、生成文件和日志必须一致；不得复制参考输出或把作者已有结果标成此次重新推断结果。同一根源错误不重复处罚机械传导的下游数值，但独立缺失的工作仍须单独记录。

执行与边界
闭卷，只使用原题input_files中的现有公开原件，均为只读；不需要外部资料检索、付费数据库、GPU、重新训练或全量重新推断。本题所给代码引用的神经分类器权重并未随现有输入提供，因此本版强制的是现有原件支持的预处理、复核及分流工具实际运行，不把缺失权重的模型推断列为必做，也不能将它宣称为已经完成。不得补造判决、标注、实验结果或客户事实；对原件未包含的内容只能明确范围限制。分流规则、阈值和精读取样规则须在评估前固定并保存配置；合理不同的方案和有据的不同法律结论均可接受。交付使用中文，案名和必要引文保留英文。
本题是基于真实公开研究材料的AI研究版工作模拟，不代表论文作者或真实客户的委托，也不属于禁止AI作者的正式外发专家题包。

1.1 Code: Formal
1.1.1 DESCRIPTION:
A legal decision made according to a rule, often viewing the law as a closed and
mechanical system. It screens the decision-maker off from the political, social, and
economic choices involved in the decision.


1.1.2 CORE EXAMPLES:
Accepting this point, too, for argument’s sake, the question becomes: What did
"discriminate" mean in 1964? As it turns out, it meant then roughly what it means
today: "To make a difference in treatment or favor (of one as compared with others)."
Webster’s New International Dictionary 745 (2d ed. 1954). To "discriminate against"
a person, then, would seem to mean treating that individual worse than others who
are similarly situated. [CITE]. In so-called "disparate treatment" cases like today’s, this
Court has also held that the difference in treatment based on sex must be intentional.
See, e.g., [CITE]. So, taken together, an employer who intentionally treats a person
worse because of sex—such as by firing the person for actions or attributes it would
tolerate in an individual of another sex—discriminates against that person in violation
of Title VII. Bostock v. Clayton County

1.2.1 DESCRIPTION:

production and improvement of decisions that make sense on their face and in light
of political, social, and economic factors.

Respondent’s argument is not without force. But it overlooks the significance of the
              relationship between jurisprudence and ideology? Should we regard jurisprudential
              commitments as merely justificatory frameworks for ideological positions? Or is the
              relationship between these concepts more complicated? Likewise, does jurisprudence
              exert independent causal effect on case outcomes (or social outcomes more broadly)?
              Our hope is that scholars will use the measure and related datasets to deepen our
              knowledge of these and other areas.
                  Elsewhere, we have begun to apply this measure to some of the substantive questions
              noted earlier (Stiglitz and Thalken 2024, 2026). Our aim in this paper is to detail
              strategies underlying the measure of jurisprudence, to make the final measure available
              to the research community, and to release our final, fine-tuned model and intermediate
              human-annotated dataset. That intermediate dataset required hundreds of hours of
              labor to create, as described below, and will be of interest both to social scientists
              seeking to develop even more advanced measures of jurisprudence and to natural
              language processing researchers seeking to study the performance of models in a
              complex domain unlikely to be tainted by model pre-training.
                  The objective of this paper is to detail our measurement strategy and to release

            Legal reasoning
            Our study focuses on formalist versus anti-formalist legal reasoning. These modes of
            legal reasoning, called macro-jurisprudence elsewhere, describe the general approach of
            a judge to law and its interpretation (Stiglitz and Thalken 2024).1 Macro-jurisprudence
            is evident in the written opinion of a judicial decision, where the judge explains how they
            reached their holdings. For this reason, court opinions serve as valuable records of legal
            reasoning.
                Table 1 defines the two categories of legal reasoning we examine: formalism and
            anti-formalism, the latter of which we refer to using Llewellyn’s term of grand
            reasoning (Llewellyn 1960). When using formal reasoning, a judge regards the law
            as a closed, logical, and objective device for producing legal determinations. Prom-
            inent examples of formalism include textualism and originalism. At least in outward
            aspiration, textualism reaches for the formalist ideal by carefully parsing public,
            authoritative legal documents and using third-party dictionaries to uncover meaning
            (Pierce 1995); originalism does the same by finding meaning in the public under-
            standing of authoritative legal documents when they were passed, which in principle
            might be assessed empirically through contemporary commentary or other docu-
            ments (Scalia et al. 1997; Kay 2009). Distinctive characteristics of formalism include a
            deductive, almost “mechanical” (Pound 1908), method of reasoning, with a closed
            system of what counts as evidence of meaning, requiring the judge to exclude external
            factors in decision-making (Schauer 1988; Wiecek 2001). Legal meaning tends to be
            fixed and resistant to change under formalism.
                In contrast, anti-formalism or “grand” reasoning views the law as evolving across
            time and responsive to the social, political, and economic needs of the historical

            the beginning of our dataset (1870) and through at least World War I; grand
            reasoning to rise in popularity during the early-to-mid 20th century, and then
            formalism to resurge in the 1980s into the present. To assess these historical
            assumptions, we take the predictions from the model at the opinion level, find the
            normalized average between formal (1) and grand (-1) reasoning across all para-
            graphs. We then calculate an average across all opinions issued in a year.
               Our results support the core expectations of the legal historians (Figure 9).
            Formalism does, in fact, dominate from the 1870s and through the 1930s. There is
            then a rapid shift to grand reasoning following the judicial revolution of 1937, which
            remains dominant until the 1980s. Formalism surges during the 1980s and remains
            the primary mode of legal reasoning through all remaining years in our dataset,
            ending in 2024.
               Though these results support prior qualitative assessments regarding the general
            arc of legal reasoning, legal scholars disagree on the exact turning points when legal
            reasoning shifted from one form of reasoning to another. For example, legal scholars
            variously expect the early 20th-century shift from formalism to grand reasoning to
            have occurred as early as Lochner v. New York (Horwitz 1992; Schauer 1988), around
            World War I (Llewellyn 1960; Gilmore 2015; Kennedy 2006), or decades later, at the
            “judicial revolution” of 1937 (Wiecek 2001; Tamanaha 2008).
               With the granular data provided by our model’s predictions, we can identify more
            exact turning points. In particular, more than any other year, the judicial revolution
            of 1937 occurred alongside an abrupt change in legal reasoning, from the formal to
            the grand reasoning. This result is visualized in Figure 9, and prior work has evaluated
            this turning point in detail and found that it is a statistically significant turning point
            (Stiglitz and Thalken 2024).

 prep_predictions.py import pandas as pd
import os
import json
import re
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize
from eyecite import get_citations

def load_file(file_name):
    """
    Read in pre-filtered data file.
    """
    parsed_data = []
    with open(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), 'data', file_name)) as f:
        for line in f:
            parsed_data.append(line)
    return parsed_data

def clean_text(text):
    """
    Clean strings with multiple numbers and asterisks. 
    """
    text = re.sub("(\*+\d+)", "", text)
    text = re.sub("(\.\d+)", ".", text)
    return text

def find_and_replace_citations(text):
    """
    Use the eyecite package to find citations of court cases. 
    For every citation identified, replace with "CITE".
    """
    try:
        citations = get_citations(text)
        new_text = text
        for citation in citations:
            new_text = re.sub(citation.matched_text(), "CITE", new_text)
    except:
        new_text = text
    return new_text


def check_for_close_substrings(string):
    """
    Check for tokens that occur close (between 200 characters) to each other as a proxy 
    for whether a statute is interpreted. 
    """
    check_1 = re.search(r'(statute|legislation|\sact[\.|\s|,|;]).{0,200}(mean|constru|interpret|reading|understand)', string.lower())
    check_2 = re.search(r'(constru|interpret|reading|understand|mean).{0,200}(statute|legislation|\sact[\.|\s|,|;])', string.lower())
    return any([check_1, check_2])

def convert_to_clean_df(data_dic): # new function
    """
    Preprocess the text, including finding opinion-level data and replacing citations with "CITE".
    """
    new_l = []
    case_count = 0
    for case in data_dic:

        case = json.loads(case)
        # collect necessary case metadata
        case_id = case["id"]
        case_url = case["url"]
        case_name = case["name"]
        date = case["decision_date"]
        court_url = case["court"]["url"]
        citation = case["citations"]

        soup = BeautifulSoup(case["casebody"]["data"], "html.parser")
        opinions = soup.find_all("opinion") 
        print(f"opinion number: {len(opinions)}")
        opinion_count = 0
        for opinion in opinions:
            # collect necessary opinion metadata
            opinion_type = opinion["type"]
            opinion_text = opinion.text
            pretty_text = find_and_replace_citations(opinion_text)
            pretty_text = clean_text(pretty_text)
            word_count = len(word_tokenize(pretty_text))
            close_stat_interp = check_for_close_substrings(pretty_text)

            author_names = []
            author_ids = []
            authors = opinion.find_all("author")
            print(f"author number: {len(authors)}")
            for author in authors:
                author_name = author.text
                author_id = author["id"]
                author_names.append(author_name)
                author_ids.append(author_id)
            
            opinion_dict = {
                "case_id":case_id,
                "proj_case_id": case_count,
                "proj_opinion_id":opinion_count,
                "proj_id": f"{case_count}_{opinion_count}",
                "case_url":case_url,
                "case_name":case_name,
                "citations": citation,
                "date":date,
                "court_url":court_url,
                "opinion_type":opinion_type,
                "opinion_text":opinion_text,
                "pretty_text":pretty_text,
                "word_count":word_count,
                "close_stat_interp":close_stat_interp,
                "authors_raw":authors,
                "author_names":author_names,
                "author_ids":author_ids
            }

            new_l.append(opinion_dict)
            opinion_count += 1
            case_count += 1
    df = pd.DataFrame(new_l)
    return df


def split_to_paragraphs(df):
    """
    Split at the paragraph level and keep only paragraphs greater than 200 characters long. 
    """
    paragraph_df = df.assign(split_text=df['pretty_text'].str.split('\n')).explode('split_text')
    paragraph_df = paragraph_df.loc[paragraph_df['split_text'].str.len() > 200]
    paragraph_df = paragraph_df.rename(columns = {"split_text": "paragraph"})
    paragraph_df['sequence']=paragraph_df.groupby('id').cumcount()
    paragraph_df["section_id"] = paragraph_df.apply(lambda x: str(x["id"]) + "_" + str(x["sequence"]), axis = 1)
    paragraph_df["par_word_count"] = paragraph_df.apply(lambda x: len(word_tokenize(x["paragraph"])), axis = 1)
    return paragraph_df

def count_grand_seeds(df): 
    """
    Return words/phrases found in paragraph that are likely grand. 
    """
    p_report_phrases = ["conference report", "committee report", "senate report", "house report", "assembly report"]
    p_talk_words = ["senate hearing", "house hearing", "assembly hearing", "committee hearing", "conference hearing", "floor debate"]
    p_misc_words = ["legislative history", "history of the legislation", "conference committee", "joint committee", "senate committee", "house committee", "assembly committee"]
    p_social_words = ["legislative purpose", "congressional purpose", "purpose of congress", "purpose of the legislature", "social", "society"]

    p_words = p_report_phrases + p_talk_words + p_misc_words + p_social_words

    words_in_paragraph = [term for term in p_words if term in df["paragraph"].lower()]

    return words_in_paragraph 

def count_formal_seeds(df): 
    """
    Return words/phrases found in paragraph that are likely formal. 
    """
    t_dict_words = ["dictionary", "dictionarium", "liguae britannicae", "world book", "funk \& wagnalls"]
    t_grammar_words = ["expressio", "expresio", "inclusio", "noscitur a sociis", "noscitur a socis", "ejusdem generis", "last antecedent", "plain language"]
    t_substantive_words = ["whole act", "whole-act", "whole code", "whole-code", "in pari materia", "meaningful variation", "consistent usage", "surplusage", "superfluit"]
    t_formal_words = ["plain meaning", "ordinary meaning", "word"]

    t_words = t_dict_words + t_grammar_words + t_substantive_words + t_formal_words

    words_in_paragraph = [term for term in t_words if term in df["paragraph"].lower()]

    return words_in_paragraph 

def main():
    data = load_file('filtered_data.jsonl')
    longer_cases_df = convert_to_clean_df(data)
    paragraph_df = split_to_paragraphs(longer_cases_df)

    paragraph_df["formal_words"] = paragraph_df.apply(count_formal_seeds, axis = 1)
    paragraph_df["grand_words"] = paragraph_df.apply(count_grand_seeds, axis = 1)
    paragraph_df["grand_count"] = paragraph_df.apply(lambda x: len(x["grand_words"]), axis = 1)
    paragraph_df["formal_count"] = paragraph_df.apply(lambda x: len(x["formal_words"]), axis = 1)

    paragraph_df["diff"] = paragraph_df["formal_count"] - paragraph_df["grand_count"] 
    paragraph_df["diff_percent"] = paragraph_df["diff"] / paragraph_df["par_word_count"]
    
    print("Saving data.")
    paragraph_df.to_csv(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), 'data', 'data_for_predictions.csv'))

    return paragraph_df

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

            Low confidence annotations
            During the annotation process, some paragraphs had such unclear legal reasoning
            that the annotator could not confidently assign a label without a group discussion of
            the paragraph. We added the “low confidence” label so that an annotator could signal
            this lack of certainty; this label could only be added in addition to the three primary
            classes.
               If a paragraph received the low confidence label, the annotation team would
            deliberate the best label for the paragraph until forming consensus. Often, paragraphs
            with the low confidence label engage in an internal argument: for example, the
            paragraph might critique grand reasoning, but for the further improvement of that
            type of reasoning, not to promote formal reasoning. In these instances, we asked
            annotators to assign a label based solely on the paragraph text and to avoid making
            assumptions about the role of the paragraph in the entire opinion. Some of the
            peripheral examples in the codebook were added after discussing these low-confidence
            paragraphs (see Appendix).


            Ending the annotation task
            Annotation tasks are costly in terms of the time and energy of the annotators, as well
            as their compensation for performing the task. Every annotator in our project was
            also a law student, so we were careful to end the annotation task when the marginal
            improvement of additional training data became low. More data would certainly be
            better, as it would allow for more partitioning and testing of the models, but that must

tasks.instruction:
金融危机模型独立验证：机制证据、预测授权与政策证据分层（修订草案 R4 · 运行与结果验证）

目标
你是金融机构模型风险团队的独立验证负责人。委员会考虑将 Krishnamurthy 与 Li《Dissecting Mechanisms of Financial Crises: Intermediation and Sentiment》的框架用于危机预警研究和逆周期资本政策讨论。请基于现有公开年度模拟路径、表格、代码和基准MAT，判断两种预期机制各自支持什么研究结论，选择或否决一个具体预警方案，并划清资本支持政策讨论的证据边界。不能只交回归汇总，也不能以“有条件研究试用”结束而不处置验证中实际出现的冲突。该委托为合成场景，材料均来自作者网站和 Harvard Dataverse，不代表真实机构委托。

必须完成的验证（结果要求，方法自选）
0. 可运行的Python工程。须在隔离环境中安装或配置依赖，建立统一入口，实际运行Bayesian和Diagnostic两组路径的全部本题可计算验证模块及上述预测设定，不能只交模型公式、伪代码或运行一套后复制结果。允许将作者R/Stata逻辑迁移为Python，但须给出来源脚本/函数与实际实现的对应，以及必要修正。固定配置并保存每阶段真实日志、输入/输出校验和异常；软件包安装可使用本机缓存或包源，研究资料不超出给定原件。这里的“运行预测设定”指实际拟合及预测，不是读取作者发布系数。

1. 数据与变量账本。核对论文版本（2025期刊发表、2023作者工作稿、2024复制包）与两份年度路径的完整性。报告中使用的每个变量，须先从作者代码确认其时间跨度、单位和缩放方式再使用，并在变量账本中给出对应代码位置；能由原始状态变量推出的量须独立重算并与存储列逐行对账。
2. 作者发布数值的独立复算。逐项登记论文Table3、附录TableA1及校准目标表的数值，先区分模型模拟结果、实际市场比较值和校准目标。对现有年度路径支持的两模型结果须全部独立复算，包括TableA1两模型各七项及Table3六类关系；另实际运行Main_Step3.do对应的两种预测设定，分别给出Bayesian与Diagnostic模型的拟合结果、概率效果及有效样本。原实证样本未随包提供的市场比较值只能核查来源和手工登记/覆盖过程；依赖缺失月度路径或其他原件的校准量须定位其依赖及无法复算的原因，不能伪称由年度路径复原，也不能因此跳过其余可计算项。逐项对账表须记录来源定位、模型版本、估计式、样本、单位、作者值、自算值、差异及处置。相同公式/样本的确定性统计绝对误差不超过1e-6；两位小数发布表允许0.0051。优化估计及随机模拟另声明有依据的收敛/抽样容差并提供诊断。超差须定位实现、统计定义或版本原因；有据不同口径可被接受，不能只以“存在差异”结束，也不得直接推断论文错误。区分目标内拟合和目标外检验，并判断两模型差异能否归因于预期机制。
3. 代码与论文一致性审查。审查作者分析代码与政策代码中的系数、参数、窗口和输出变量的实际定义是否与论文及表注表述一致；对每处不一致，在原件支持的范围内实际量化对样本、估计值或授权结论的影响；不支持重算的部分须指出具体缺失依赖及受影响主张。手工登记的市场比较系数不得当作模型估计，不得把取消覆盖后得到的模拟拟合冒称真实市场重估。
4. 危机事件与稳健性。从原始路径重建危机前、当年与危机后的信贷与GDP路径；必须同时完成“事件定义变化”和“预测窗口变化”两类敏感性，并实测事件重叠的影响，报告效果量、样本边界与时间依赖的不确定性。危机前窗口另做至少一种合理变化；每项比较保存基准与变更设定的样本、事件定位和结果，不能只描述将来打算如何验证。
5. 预警方案。形成一个只使用现实可观测输入的预警方案及合适的简单基准，在模拟时间顺序上做留出检验，保证标签与数据依赖的选择不跨越训练边界；报告概率质量、选定操作点的漏报/误报与处理负担，以及选定预警方案相对简单基准的关键增量。该增量须在同一留出样本上作配对的时间依赖推断，并检验一种合理关键设定变化下结论是否稳定；保存增量值、区间、配置和明细。仅给低利差组风险差的区间不能替代预警增量验证；负增量或不显著也可形成有效的否决证据。明确模拟留出不等于真实市场样本外验证。
6. 授权决定。用一张“主张—支持证据—相反证据—授权用途”表，把机制研究、生产预警、资本政策讨论三种用途对应到本轮实际结果，每条结论都要指向可定位的数值来源；至少对一条关键主张，将支持结果与实际相反结果或可检验限制放在可比的样本/估计对象下定量核验，保存输出并解释其支持范围。没有相反结果时提交实际执行的相关压力检验，不制造反例，也不以通用风险清单代替；至少处置一个实际出现的对账或效果冲突，若确无冲突须展示完整核对证明。
7. 政策证据边界。说明跨模型如何匹配经济状态、政策实验实际改变什么、政策输出实际衡量什么；区分可直接复算的量、需从现有代码重建的量和仍未建立的量，以及取得何种额外证据后才能授权使用。无需重建完整动态均衡或新的政策路径，但不能只写“缺更多数据”。自然路径分箱不能冒充政策处理效应。

交付
危机模型独立验证报告.docx；模型验证证据.xlsx；可在空输出目录重建核心数表的代码、配置和运行说明；机器可读的对账表、主张证据表及每项估计的样本/事件年度定位。另外提交环境安装说明或脚本、锁定版本的依赖清单、原作者逻辑到Python实现的对应表、完整运行日志及机器可读的模块执行清单；每个必做模块须有实际状态、有效样本和输出位置。提供一条空输出目录重建命令，以及从逐记录计算/样本明细检查汇总对账的验收入口，记录实际比较值，不能只输出预写的“通过”。报告关键结论必须引用本次运行产物；报告不能代替缺失的拟合、对账或机器输出。同一根源错误不重复处罚机械下游数值，独立缺失的模块仍须记录。运行验收分别检查四类证据：实际环境配置与版本记录；作者代码到Python的可追溯适配；两模型全部必做模块的执行覆盖与真实日志；独立产物验收入口的实际结果。允许复用已有隔离环境或缓存，无须反复下载安装。仅列依赖、贴作者文件名、检查文件存在或预写“通过”都不能代替相应证据。模块清单须包含A1、Table3六类关系、Step3两种设定、事件及敏感性、留出预警和增量验证；每种源probit设定在两模型分别拟合并保存收敛/数值诊断。验收可以使用分离的检查入口或独立来源对账，不要求重复编写另一套业务程序。

评分结构：42条独立二元项，正权重合计217；其中核心计算与运行验证180权重，约82.95%。完整A1计算、A1对账和Step3拟合分别为10、8、10权重；四类运行验收分别为4、6、10、8权重。其余权重及逐条通过边界见同目录rubrics.json。没有隐藏总分封顶；同一根源数值错误不在机械下游重复处罚，独立缺失工作单独记录。说明版本、依赖、随机种子、单位及数值容差。可用等价工具、估计方法、留出比例和敏感性规则。

边界
闭卷，仅使用原题 public/input_files；不要求安装Matlab/Stata，给定分析与预测设定须用Python实际执行；不要求用当前缺少完整依赖的精选输入包重新求解动态均衡。完整均衡求解和新政策轨迹若未运行，必须明确未完成，不能以运行年度路径回归来冒称两套结构模型已经重求解。无需付费数据或外部资料搜索。作者模拟是真实公开研究产物而非现实市场记录；经验数值若只能在作者代码中找到引用或手工登记，须标明证据等级，不能冒称已从原始实证数据复现。所有输入只读，不得编造实际市场外部验证或因果政策证据。即使否决生产准入，也必须完成上述验证。中文交付。AI研究版，不代表专家署名验收。

reg_crises_predictability <- function(TB, auxiliary=FALSE){
  TB_yearly = TB

  TB_yearly[ , froth := credit_spread<=quantile(credit_spread,cutoff) ]
  TB_yearly[ , crisis_next_year :=  c(  crisis[2:nrow(TB_yearly)]>0,  NA  ) ]

  TB_yearly[ , high_credit_past_5y := c( rep(0,4), rollmean(high_credit,5 ) )>0 ]
  TB_yearly[ , capital_crash := capital_excess_return<quantile(capital_excess_return,0.05) ]
  marginal_effect <- function(reg){
    summary_results = summary(margins(reg))
    return(as.numeric(summary_results[2])*100)
  }
  
  regs = list()
  regs[[1]] = glm( crisis_next_3_year ~ froth, family = binomial(), data = TB_yearly)
  regs[[2]] = glm( crisis_next_year ~ bank_credit_GDP, family = binomial(), data = TB_yearly)
  # 
  regs[[1]]$coefficients[2] = marginal_effect(regs[[1]])
  regs[[2]]$coefficients[2] = marginal_effect(regs[[2]])
  return(regs)

gen_basic_definitions <- function(TB){
  # TB[ , bank_credit_GDP := bank_credit/GDP ]   # Note: this definition is equivalent
  TB[ , bank_credit_GDP := w*(xK-1)*p/(productivity) ]
  TB[ , total_bank_equity := w*p*K ]

# Then define some risk premium measures. 
gen_risk_premium_measures <- function(TB, sigmaK){
  TB[, risk_premium:=lambda*(kappap+alpha)/(1-xK*kappap-alpha*(xK-1)) + (vol_of_p+sigmaK)^2*xK]
  TB[, total_risk_unadjusted:=lambda*(kappap+alpha)^2 + (vol_of_p+sigmaK)^2 ]
  TB[, total_bank_equity_risks:=(total_risk_unadjusted) * xK^2 ]
  TB[,dw_quadratic_var:=lambda*(xK*kappap+alpha*pmax(xK-1,0))^2 + (vol_of_p+sigmaK)^2*xK^2 ]
  TB[,total_Sharpe:=risk_premium/sqrt(total_risk_unadjusted)]  # This is the total Sharpe ratio.
  return(TB)
}

gen_crisis <- function(TB, cutoff=NA){
  TB[ , Year:= floor(T) ]
  # Define financial crisis based on equity returns.
  gen_non_clustered_crisis <- function( crisis_vec ){
    diff_vec = diff(which(crisis_vec==1))
    crisis_sparse = crisis_vec
    crisis_last = which(crisis_vec)[1]
    for( index in which(crisis_vec)[2:length(diff_vec)] ){
      if(index-crisis_last<0*12){   # 3 years of non consecutive crises
        crisis_sparse[index] = 0
      }else{
        crisis_sparse[index] = 1
        crisis_last = index
      }
    }
    return(crisis_sparse)
  }
  credit_monthly_growth = c(diff(TB$bank_credit_GDP), 0) / TB$bank_credit_GDP
  equity_monthly_change = TB$equity_monthly_change
  solve_for_cutoff <- function(cutoff){
    if(crisis_def == "bank_credit_GDP_change"){
      crisis_vec = credit_monthly_growth < cutoff
    }else{   # equity crisis
      crisis_vec = equity_monthly_change < cutoff
    }
    crisis_sparse = gen_non_clustered_crisis(crisis_vec)
    DT = data.table( Year=TB$Year, crisis_sparse )
    crisis_sparse_yearly = DT[ , list(crisis_sparse=mean(crisis_sparse)>0), by=Year ]$crisis_sparse
    return( mean(crisis_sparse_yearly) - 0.04 )
  }
  if(is.na(cutoff)){
    result = uniroot(solve_for_cutoff, lower=quantile(credit_monthly_growth,0.001), upper=quantile(credit_monthly_growth,0.5)   )
    cutoff=result$root
  }
  if(crisis_def == "bank_credit_GDP_change"){
    print( paste0("Crisis cut off for bank credit growth is ", round(cutoff,digits=2) ) )
    TB[ , crisis := gen_non_clustered_crisis(credit_monthly_growth < cutoff) ]
  }else{  # equity crisis
    print( paste0("Crisis cut off for bank equity growth is ", round(cutoff,digits=2) ) )
    TB[ , crisis := gen_non_clustered_crisis(equity_monthly_change < cutoff) ]
  }
  return(TB)
}
m_fun <- function(x){
  # return(  x[ floor(length(x)/2)+1 ]  )
  return(  first(x)  )
}
gen_yearly_data <- function(TB){
  TB[ , Year:= floor(T) ]
  TB[ , p_yearly_return:= c( rep(NA,12), p[13:nrow(TB)]/p[1:(nrow(TB)-12)] - 1    ) ]
  TB[ ,p_vol_empirical := c(NA, roll_sd( p[2:nrow(TB)]/p[1:(nrow(TB)-1)] - 1 , width=12)) ]
  TB[is.na(p_vol_empirical) ,p_vol_empirical := mean_fun(p_vol_empirical) ]  # For the initial 12 NA observations, just replace them with average volatility. 
  TB[ ,p_vol_empirical := p_vol_empirical/mean_fun(p_vol_empirical) ]
 TB[ , K_monthly_growth := c(rep(0,1), logK_vec_original[2:nrow(TB)]-logK_vec_original[1:(nrow(TB)-1)] )  ]
  TB[ , K_monthly_growth := winsorize(K_monthly_growth, lower_quantile=0.001, upper_quantile=0.999)  ]
  TB[, capital_return_monthly :=  c( rep(NA,1) , K_monthly_growth[2:nrow(TB)] + log(p[2:nrow(TB)]/p[1:(nrow(TB)-1)]) )  ]
  # Define the monthly return volatilty, in yearly unit (i.e., think about the continuous-time limit of the volatility on sample path)
  TB[, capital_return_vol_simulation := c( rep(NA,12) , 12*roll_sd( capital_return_monthly[13:nrow(TB)] , width=12)  )  ]
  TB[is.na(capital_return_vol_simulation) , capital_return_vol_simulation := mean_fun(capital_return_vol_simulation) ]
  TB_qunatities = TB[ , list( Year, dN, crisis, total_bank_equity )  ]
  TB_yearly_quantities = TB_qunatities[, lapply(.SD, mean,na.rm=TRUE), by=Year]
  # deal with some outliers due to numerical issues
  TB[rK_monthly_from_sim>quantile(TB$rK_monthly_from_sim,0.999,na.rm=TRUE)]$rK_monthly_from_sim = NA
  TB[,rK_yearly:= exp(rollsum( log(1+rK_monthly_from_sim), 12, fill=NA, align="right")) - 1  ]
  TB_yearly_prices = TB[ , list(  Year, w, xK, lambda, lambda_rational, underlying_lambda, K, GDP, productivity, bank_equity, vol_of_p, dB_premia, bank_credit,
                                  p, credit_spread, rf, rK, rd, equity_excess_return,  sharpe_ratio, investment_rate,  capital_excess_return, p_vol_empirical, kappap, p_yearly_return, 
                                  bank_credit_GDP, rK_yearly, logK_vec_original, total_Sharpe, risk_premium, total_risk_unadjusted, capital_return_vol_simulation) ]
  # Note: the variable "investment rate" maps to phi(mu^K) in the model, which is the cost of investment, or the real resources cost by investment. 
  TB_yearly_prices = TB_yearly_prices[ , lapply(.SD, first), by=Year ]
  TB_yearly = merge(TB_yearly_quantities, TB_yearly_prices, by="Year")
  TB_yearly[ , crisis:=crisis>0 ]
  TB_yearly[ , dN:=dN>0 ]
  return( TB_yearly[ Year>=1 ] )
}

processing_simulation_data <- function(TB_yearly){
  # Note: the input table should be at yearly frequency
  TB_yearly[ , bank_credit_GDP_pre_year :=  c( mean(bank_credit_GDP),  bank_credit_GDP[1:(nrow(TB_yearly)-1)]   )   ]
  TB_yearly[, bank_equity_excess_return:= equity_excess_return]
  TB_yearly[ , sigma_of_p_standardized := vol_of_p/mean(vol_of_p)  ]
  TB_yearly[ , total_vol_standardized :=  sqrt(total_risk_unadjusted) / mean_fun(sqrt(total_risk_unadjusted)) ]   # Standardize the theory-implied total volatility 
  weights = 0.8^c(10:0)
  TB_yearly[ , historical_vol_p := roll_sd(p, 10, weights ) ]
  TB_yearly[ is.na(historical_vol_p)]$historical_vol_p = mean(TB_yearly$historical_vol_p,na.rm=TRUE)
  TB_yearly[ , Kp := K*p ]
  TB_yearly[ , capital_growth := c( K[2:nrow(TB_yearly)]/K[1:(nrow(TB_yearly)-1)]-1, 0 ) ]
  TB_yearly[ , investment_rate_3Y:=  c( rollsum( investment_rate, 3 ), rep( 3*mean(TB_yearly$investment_rate) ,2)) ]
  index = 1:(nrow(TB_yearly)-1)
  # Next-year capital return
  # Average credit spread: the average last 5 year value of credit spread, following Krishnamurthy and Muir definition
  TB_yearly[ , avg_credit_spread_5Y := c( rep(0,5-1), rollmean(credit_spread, k=5) )  ]
  TB_yearly[,  froth:= avg_credit_spread_5Y<median(avg_credit_spread_5Y)]  # This is the definition in KM 2017.
  crises_index = which( TB_yearly$crisis==1 )

   Lastly, we ask the question, does it matter for policy purposes whether we are living
in a world with diagnostic beliefs or one with Bayesian beliefs? It is well understood that
in models with financial frictions, leverage restrictions can improve welfare by alleviating a
pecuniary externality. See Bianchi (2011) for example. Our model fits within this framework.
When agents have distorted beliefs, leverage policies can also improved welfare under a
paternalistic welfare criterion. See Dávila and Walther (2020). Thus in our model, it is
interesting to study a leverage restriction and ask how the nature of beliefs affects policy
assessment.

    We consider an unexpected policy that transfers wealth from households to bankers so
that the banker wealth share increases by 10% during a pre-crisis boom period. The policy
captures the impact of increasing bank equity (or equivalently, reducing bank leverage) to
lean-against-the-wind, along the lines of Gertler, Kiyotaki and Prestipino (2020). Under each

and map these into the state variables in each model (they map to different values of the state
variable across the models). We then simulate the path of the economy with and without
the recapitalization policy. We calculate the difference in quantities and prices between the
with- and without-recapitalization and repeat this across both models. Our main finding
is that these impulse response differences are quite similar across both models. The policy
raises the mean path of output and credit, and the conditional response of these variables to
an illiquidity shock, but these responses are quantitatively similar across both models. The
two keys to this similarity result are that (1) both models are calibrated to common data
but are not forced to having a common parameterization, and (2) both models are tied to
the same initial condition in terms of observables. In particular, the diagnostic model does
not just take the Bayesian model parameters and add a new diagnostic parameter. In this
case, which is not economically meaningful, the impulse responses are no longer similar.

The challenge of solving this model comes from both multiple state variables and the en-

method that begins with an initial guess of the capital price function p(0) (w, λ), and then
iterates over the equilibrium equation system to get an updated price p(1) . This updating
step involves solving a fixed-point problem at each state (w, λ). Then we iterate until at

frequency to be consistent with the data.

• Once shocks are generated, we solve for the dynamics of state variables, including wt , λt ,

• With state variables determined, we generate all other quantities and prices of the model.

• We discard the first one thousand data points of each simulation path collected in this

4      Calibration

In order to map model outputs to data, we need to define a financial crisis. Crises are the
events where the growth in bank credit/GDP in a given month falls into the lowest 4%
quantile of the distribution of monthly bank credit/GDP growth rates, and there has not
been another such event in the previous three years. This latter criterion is to ensure that a
longer crisis is still dated as a single crisis, as is done in the empirical literature. This crisis


                                                     26
 corresponds to a disintermediation event, and in the simulation almost always involves an
illiquidity shock and bank run, although as crises are endogenous, not all illiquidity events
are crises. We target the 4% number based on fact 1 of Section 2. We also consider a crisis
definition based on bank equity crashes, as in Baron and Xiong (2017), in Section 5.8.

   We solve and calibrate three variants of the model:

1. Bayesian (rational) Model: Agents form beliefs over the illiquidity state following Bayes
   rule, and this belief varies over time.

2. Diagnostic (non-rational) Model: Agents form beliefs over the illiquidity state via diag-
   nostic expectations, and belief varies over time.

3. Static-belief Model: Agents’ beliefs are constant.

   We apply a combination of calibration and estimation for model parameters. Specifically,
we directly set parameter values for those with standard values in the literature. Then we
estimate the rest of parameters based on moments chosen to best reflect the economics of
those parameters.

6     Policy Impact under Diagnostic and Bayesian Beliefs

We have shown that a financial friction mechanism plus a belief mechanism can capture the
main features of the crisis cycle. We also learn that both the Bayesian and diagnostic belief
models work, with the diagnostic model generating over-sensitivity relative to the data for
the crisis and post-crisis patterns, while the Bayesian model is under-sensitive in its fit of
the pre-crisis froth. Our take on these results, generated from a fairly parsimonious model,
is that nailing down the source of belief fluctuations is not essential to a researcher aiming
to match the main patterns of the crisis cycle.

    We next turn to evaluating our model’s implications for a policy experiment. We ask,
does it matter for policy purposes whether we live in a world with diagnostic beliefs or
one with Bayesian beliefs? We run the following experiment: we start the economy in
a boom state (time t = 0) with low credit spread and high leverage, and then consider
an unexpected policy that transfers wealth from households to bankers so that the banker
wealth share w0 increases by 10%. The idea is to recapitalize banks to “lean against the
wind” so that the severity of a crisis is reduced if an illiquidity shock dNt hits. This exercise
is similar to Gertler, Kiyotaki and Prestipino (2020). Under each version of the model, we
calculate the “derivative” of the nonlinear impulse response of quantities and asset prices
with respect to the recapitalization policy. We focus on aggregate variables to assess the
